name: Hexagons
description: Lindsey Buckingham told Stevie Nicks "Go your own way" . Nicks is now sad and wants to go away as quickly as possible, but she lives in a 2D hexagonal world. Consider a hexagonal tiling of the plane as on the picture below. Nicks wishes to go from the cell marked $$$(0, 0)$$$ to a certain cell given by the coordinates. She may go from a hexagon to any of its six neighbors you want, but there is a cost associated with each of them. The costs depend only on the direction in which you travel. Going from $$$(0, 0)$$$ to $$$(1, 1)$$$ will take the exact same cost as going from $$$(-2, -1)$$$ to $$$(-1, 0)$$$. The costs are given in the input in the order $$$c_1$$$, $$$c_2$$$, $$$c_3$$$, $$$c_4$$$, $$$c_5$$$, $$$c_6$$$ as in the picture below. Print the smallest cost of a path from the origin which has coordinates $$$(0, 0)$$$ to the given cell.
input_specification: Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 10^{4}$$$). Description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains two integers $$$x$$$ and $$$y$$$ ($$$-10^{9} \le x, y \le 10^{9}$$$) representing the coordinates of the target hexagon. The second line of each test case contains six integers $$$c_1$$$, $$$c_2$$$, $$$c_3$$$, $$$c_4$$$, $$$c_5$$$, $$$c_6$$$ ($$$1 \le c_1, c_2, c_3, c_4, c_5, c_6 \le 10^{9}$$$) representing the six costs of the making one step in a particular direction (refer to the picture above to see which edge is for each value).
output_specification: For each testcase output the smallest cost of a path from the origin to the given cell.
approach_summary: Formulate the state transition graph with non-negative weights. Execute Dijkstra's algorithm with priority queue to find shortest paths in O((V + E) log V).

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1421D — Hexagons [168. Dijkstra's Algorithm]
topic_editorial.summary: Single-source shortest path using Dijkstra's algorithm.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Because all edge weights are non-negative, the shortest distance to the unvisited vertex with the minimum tentative distance is finalized and cannot be decreased by further transitions (greedy choice property).
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Graph Modeling
Construct an adjacency list with pairs $(v, w)$ for each directed or undirected edge from $u$ to $v$ with weight $w \ge 0$.

### Step 2: Distance Table Initialization
Initialize $dist[v] = \infty$ for all vertices, with $dist[\text{source}] = 0$.
Push $(0, \text{source})$ into a min-priority queue `std::priority_queue<pair<long long, int>, vector<pair<long long, int>>, greater<>>`.

### Step 3: Relaxation Loop
While the priority queue is not empty:
1. Pop $(d, u)$. If $d > dist[u]$, discard (stale entry).
2. For each neighbor $(v, w)$ of $u$:
   If $dist[u] + w < dist[v]$:
   $$dist[v] = dist[u] + w$$
   Push $(dist[v], v)$ into the priority queue.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((V + E) \log V)$
  Every vertex is extracted from the priority queue at most once. For every edge, we perform at most one priority queue push operation taking $\mathcal{O}(\log V)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(V + E)$
  Required for storing the adjacency list and the distance array.
